en: My own kin fired upon me;
Now I have no life to spare from death.
Since I came to Talas
To see you, my kin,
Did I hijack your field?
You have utterly exhausted my strength.
Damn you, worthless men,
Did I carry off your treasure?!
Foolish kin, may you never prosper!
Even when I offered my mother, you refused;
Saying, ‘I'll yawn, then slaughter him,’
You did not give up your wickedness.
You have now exhausted my life;
Though I took on your burdens,
I offered my head as a gift.
Even when I offered my head, you refused;
You would not cease your blustering.
Common iron is not keen steel,
Dogs raised apart are not a people.
Iron pieced together is not keen steel.
Rabid dogs are not a people.
You have coveted, forty companions,
My treasures, such as Akolpok.
When I consider it, forty companions,
You have meant to bring
This orphan to his end.
Is amusement what you seek?
Is destruction what you desire?
Is contention what you ponder?
Is battle what you want?
On the swift horse you would not give when asked,
I shall cast a cruel lasso.
You have cast me down, forty companions;
I shall offer you all as a sacrifice!
You have tormented me, forty companions;
I shall shatter you and take revenge!
Those forty choros who attacked as one,
I offered my head, but you refused.
Firing with mighty crashes,
You would not cease your mischief.
God has now struck you squarely.
He did not rein aside his steed,
Though I pleaded with you as my kin,
Here stand my enemies!
If I were to rush forward and attack,
May my father's spirit
Come straight upon me and strike me down!
Worse than beasts, you fired at me.
May Allah Most High strike you down!
I did not spill your blood;
Your father's grave, forty uncles!
You have burned my soul.
Forty uncles, here you stand.
Were you a red, jagged cliff?
Was I an enemy come from China?
Forty uncles who know no gratitude,
Were you a mountain of dark ridges?
For you to charge and attack me,
Was I an enemy come from the Kalmyks?
When I migrated from Bukhara,
I hunted wild asses and ate along the way.
Your father's grave, forty companions!
I came thinking you kin who would care for me.
Now let your guilt fall upon yourselves.
You attacked first, forty companions;
Your suffering upon your own dark crowns!
When I set out from Bukhara,
I hunted bustards and ate along the way.
I came thinking all of you, forty companions,
Would be my support.
Now watch, forty companions:
I mean to kill you,
I mean to gouge out your eyes.
I mean to drain your strength,
I mean to spill your blood!”
This was where they came to me, the unfortunate one.
He covered his exposed places.
His wrath would not subside;
Grief burned within him.
The forty companions stood firing.
When the orphan saw they would not turn back,
His eyes blazed like fire.
The offspring of the lion favored by Khizr
Was seized by a terrible fit.
His door-sized white teeth
Your orphan, the young lord,
Ground with a crash.
His wrath was plain to see.
His door-sized white teeth,
When the orphan clenched them,
Broke apart like grains of millet.
Then the Alengir bow and steel-tipped arrows,
Now he would give them a tale to tell!
That son of the oceanlike hero
Did not look about him,
And spared his life not at all.
Boz Kise, fallen from heaven,
He girded on, crying “Allah!”
Zulfiqar, left by his father Khan Manas,
He grasped by its hilt
And drew from its sheath.
In one of the orphan's hands
Was the gold-cheeked battle-axe;
Beneath the orphan's thigh
Was Syrnaiza, left by Manas.
At his right side could be seen
A gilded pouch.
Those who saw him were troubled.
Your orphan, the gray-maned hero's son,
Appeared as great as Mount Opol.
Girding on a golden belt,
Light shone upon his moonlike face.
Girding on a silver belt,
Light shone upon his sunlike face.
Growing fierce and wrathful,
His pupils blazed.
Your orphan, who knew no measure,
Was seized by thirst for blood.
The forty companions stood thrusting spears.
He struck Taibuurul once,
Leveled his spear and shouted,
Raising “Manas!” as his battle cry,
And attacked the forty companions.
The seven standards left by Manas
He planted in seven places.
Now your orphan entered the fight,
Sending men crawling wherever he reached.
The six honored standards
He planted in six places.
Your orphan drove in,
Sending them crawling from the first.
Among the mighty, Kuldur died;
He was a servant born foolish;
The hero Baichoro died.
There where he made a mighty spectacle,
Along great Kyzart,
Along broad Kochkor,
His mount a white-marked peerless steed,
Among the forty companions,
Kochkor and Chyybyt together—
The offspring of Ukuman,
The offspring of the raging one
Attacked before they could cry out.
Of the bewildered forty companions,
Six died in a single place.
Their renowned men died upon the ridge.
His elder kinsmen Kochkor and Chyybyt
Died where they came together.
Adybai and Kolbai died.
The best of the forty companions,
Precious Kuldur, died.
Tolomon's Tolgochu,
The darling of wealthy Tortkuron,
Argyn Khan's Azhybai—
The leader of the forty companions,
Korogoch, born a gray-maned hero—
Their brave leaders died here.
When their affairs went ruinously awry,
The forty companions came together,
Beseeching Semetey.
When the companions came pleading,
It smoked every time it ran out
Who blazes whenever extinguished;
The rest of the forty companions
He seized, every one.
Dragging them out upon the road,
He tore them apart for the great hounds.
Semetey was a sultan:
As though to quench his thirst,
He swallowed their blood.
The forty companions left by Manas—
With his four elder kinsmen foremost,
He slaughtered them completely.
He slaughtered the forty companions,
And only after slaughter found relief.
He set the grasslands ablaze,
And kindled the meadows.
Pouring blood into the dark waters,
He truly earned the name Bloodthirsty.
He greased the land along the rivers with blood.
When their feud grew bitter,
He slew his own elder kinsmen.
He hardened himself by shedding blood,
And won the name Bloodthirsty.
He came and settled in Talas,
Destroyed the forty companions,
And was left alone.
He had slaughtered the forty companions.
He had repaid them for their deeds,
And only after slaughter found relief.
He devoured Khan Zhakyp.
In the orphan son of Manas
Not the least regret remained.
He sent Kobosh to the grave,
And showed his gray-maned fierceness.
He struck Abyke down,
And destroyed the man himself.
He grew hardened, sated with blood.
Semetey, the Bloodthirsty One's son,
Was named the blood-drinking, gray-maned hero.
He killed the enemies who faced him.
Never to draw back from blood,
He licked his sword and swore an oath.
Killing his own close kin,
He imposed his decree upon the people.
The true news of himself, Semetey
To the khan of Chin-Machin,
Kongurbai, made known.
This orphan was twelve years old,
No ordinary one, this wily orphan.
His fame became known to the people:
“He slaughtered his elder kinsmen,” they said.
In forty-gated Beijing's
Register it was written down.
A lion had arisen who slew his elder kinsmen;
A hero had arisen to conquer the world.
Precious old Bakai,
Sary Khan and Zhamgyrchy
Quickly saddled their horses,
And were setting out,
Alarmed for their orphan.
His uncle, Lion Bakai—
Look at the wisdom of the man,
Of Bakai, the true saint,
The clarity of his judgment.
Nor charged wildly against the foe.
The narrow path of Judgment Day—
“Has he seen it?” he wondered.
“This damned orphan—
Has he died?” he wondered.
His beard grew thin,
And the tears flowing down both cheeks
Poured below his collarbones.
The forty companions left by Manas,
Forty quarrelsome companions come from forty places,
Might suddenly have begun shooting,
Might suddenly have begun fighting.
“He has not yet gone grieving into battle;
He has not yet learned an enemy's worth.
Has Semetey met them
And died?” he wondered.
The narrow path of Judgment Day—
“Has he seen it?” he wondered.
Your uncle Bakai grieved;
Look at that wolf of war!
Two khans followed him.
The Muslim could not gather his senses;
His mustache grew thin,
And water poured from his nose.
Unable to wipe his tears,
Unable to draw back his mucus,
Khan Bakai was deeply distressed.
He sped along upon Kokcholok,
Flinging hoof-clods the size of basins.
When given his head, Kokcholok
Flew onward like a shimmer.
